subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: Adapted from school Geography lesson plans in Drive: 'Geo - Y8 - 4.1 What Causes Waves and Tides', 'Geo - Y8 - 4.3 Which Landforms Do the Waves Create?', 'Geo - Y8 - 4.5 Your holiday in Newquay'; National Curriculum KS3; AQA GCSE coasts progression

lessons.title: What causes waves and tides? (4.1)
objectives: Explain how wind creates waves and what fetch is
Compare constructive and destructive waves
Explain what causes tides and the difference between spring and neap tides

keywords.def: the distance of open water over which the wind blows
the forward movement of water up a beach after a wave breaks
the movement of water back down the beach
the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the Moon
a rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong winds

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the layers of the Earth from the surface down.
What is the difference between a river's source and its mouth?
What do you think causes waves? Write your idea in one sentence.

teach.heading: How waves form
bullets: Wind blows across the surface of the sea.
Friction pushes the water into waves.
The wave breaks when it reaches shallow water.
teach.note: Start with the tray of water demonstration from the school plan: blow across the water and watch ripples form, then tilt the tray to show how water moves onto the land. Ask: what happens as you blow harder? Note the model's limits; real waves have far more energy. The water itself moves in circles; only the energy travels forward.

teach.heading: Fetch: why some waves are bigger
bullets: Fetch is the distance wind blows over open water.
Stronger wind and longer fetch make bigger waves.
The UK's south-west coast faces the Atlantic and gets big waves.
teach.note: Show a map: the Atlantic fetch is thousands of kilometres, while the North Sea fetch is shorter. This is why surfers go to Cornwall and Devon. Use the tray model: a longer tray gives a longer fetch. Ask pupils which UK coast would get the smallest waves.

teach.heading: Constructive and destructive waves
bullets: Constructive waves are low, with strong swash. They build beaches.
Destructive waves are high and steep, with strong backwash. They erode.
Constructive: about 6 to 8 per minute. Destructive: 10 to 14.
teach.note: Misconception from the school plan: pupils think waves only erode. Show diagrams of each type and stress that waves can both erode and deposit. Ask: after a storm, why might a beach lose sand? (Destructive waves take it away). Use hand movements: swash forwards, backwash back.

teach.heading: What causes tides?
bullets: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans.
Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides a day.
High tide comes about every 12 hours 25 minutes.
teach.note: Use a diagram of Earth and Moon with the bulge of water. Tides are predictable, which is why fishermen, sailors and beach walkers use tide tables. Stress that normal tide height is not caused by wind. Ask why high tide is 25 minutes later each cycle (the Moon moves around the Earth).

teach.heading: Spring and neap tides
bullets: Spring tides: Sun, Moon and Earth line up, biggest range.
Neap tides: Sun and Moon at right angles, smallest range.
The Bay of Fundy, Canada, has a tidal range of about 16 m.
teach.note: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season; the name comes from the idea of the water 'springing up'. Show the alignment diagrams. The UK's Severn estuary has one of the biggest tidal ranges in the world, around 14 m. Explain that a storm surge combined with a spring tide is the most dangerous for coastal flooding.

practice: Complete the table comparing constructive and destructive waves.
Explain why Newquay gets larger waves than Hull, using the word fetch.
independent: Draw and label a diagram of a breaking wave showing swash and backwash.
Answer questions on waves and tides using the key words.
Stretch: explain why a storm surge at a spring tide is so dangerous for coastal towns.
exit: Which type of wave builds up a beach?
lessons.homework: Write four sentences explaining how a storm could damage a coast, using at least four key words.
lessons.send: Provide a labelled wave diagram and sentence starters. EAL: use video clips and gestures for swash and backwash. Stretch: explain why some storms affect only one side of the UK.

lessons.title: Weathering and erosion: how the coast is worn away
objectives: Explain the difference between weathering and erosion
Describe four processes of wave erosion
Explain how rock type affects the rate of erosion

keywords.def: wearing away of the land by moving water, ice or wind
the breakdown of rock in place without it being moved
the force of waves pushing air and water into cracks in rock
rocks hurled by waves scraping against cliffs
rocks colliding and becoming smaller and rounder

starter: Say Bismillah. What is fetch?
Which type of wave has a strong backwash?
What causes a spring tide?

teach.heading: Weathering or erosion?
bullets: Weathering breaks rock down where it is.
Erosion wears rock away and carries it off.
Both change the shape of the coast.
teach.note: Pupils often confuse the two. Use the phrase 'weathering stays, erosion moves'. Show a cliff with rock fragments at its base. Ask: which process made the fragments (weathering) and which carried them away (waves = erosion).

teach.heading: Types of weathering
bullets: Freeze-thaw: water freezes in cracks and expands.
Chemical: rainwater reacts with rock such as limestone.
Biological: roots and animals pry rock apart.
teach.note: Demonstrate freeze-thaw with a diagram: water enters a crack, freezes (expanding by about 9%), widens the crack, melts, and repeats. Ask where freeze-thaw is more common, in the south of England or Scotland? Scotland, with colder winters. Mention that chemical weathering is stronger in warm, wet climates.

teach.heading: Four processes of wave erosion
bullets: Hydraulic action: waves force air into cracks.
Abrasion: waves throw rocks against the cliff.
Attrition: rocks collide and wear into smaller, rounder pieces.
Solution: weak acids dissolve rock such as chalk.
teach.note: Link each process to a real image: abrasion is like sandpaper, attrition is like pebbles in a washing machine. Note that attrition changes the sediment, not the cliff. Ask pupils which process would affect a limestone cliff the most (solution).

teach.heading: Rock type matters
bullets: Hard rocks like granite erode slowly.
Soft rocks like clay and sand erode quickly.
Dorset's coast has hard limestone and soft clay.
teach.note: Show a map or photo of the Dorset coast. Harder rock resists the waves while softer rock is worn back, creating headlands and bays. This will lead into the next lesson. Ask pupils which would erode faster, a cliff of Purbeck limestone or one of boulder clay. The clay.

practice: Match each erosion process to its description and a simple sketch.
Sort these into weathering or erosion: freeze-thaw, abrasion, chemical weathering, hydraulic action.
independent: Create a table of the four wave erosion processes with a definition and a drawing for each.
Explain in a paragraph how freeze-thaw weathering breaks up a cliff.
Stretch: explain why some parts of a coastline erode faster than others.
exit: Name two types of wave erosion.
What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
lessons.homework: Find an image of an eroding coast and annotate it with at least three key terms.
lessons.send: Provide a process diagram to label. EAL: act out each process (hydraulic action, abrasion) with simple actions. Stretch: investigate the effect of different rock types on erosion rates.

lessons.title: Which landforms do waves create? Erosional landforms (4.3)
objectives: Describe how headlands and bays are formed
Explain the sequence from cave to arch to stack to stump
Identify wave-cut platforms and notches

keywords.def: a piece of land sticking out into the sea
a groove cut into the base of a cliff by waves
a flat rocky area at the foot of a cliff exposed at low tide
a natural opening through a headland
a tall column of rock separated from the headland

starter: Say Bismillah. Define erosion and deposition.
Name the four processes of wave erosion.
Why do hard and soft rocks erode at different rates?

teach.heading: Headlands and bays
bullets: Hard rock sticks out as headlands.
Soft rock is eroded back to form bays.
Waves focus their energy on the headland.
teach.note: Misconception from the school plan: pupils confuse erosion and deposition. Emphasise that these landforms are made by erosion. Show a diagram of alternating hard and soft rock. Ask: which will stand out as the headland? The harder rock. Example: Swanage Bay and Ballard Down in Dorset.

teach.heading: Cliffs, notches and platforms
bullets: Waves cut a notch at the foot of the cliff.
The cliff above collapses, leaving a steep face.
The cliff retreats, leaving a wave-cut platform.
teach.note: Sketch the stages: notch, overhang, collapse, retreat. The platform is the flat area exposed at low tide, covered in rock pools. Ask pupils why rock pools are good for study (they show life adapting to tidal changes). Use annotated sketches.

teach.heading: Caves, arches, stacks and stumps
bullets: Waves widen a crack into a cave.
Caves on both sides join to make an arch.
The arch collapses, leaving a stack, then a stump.
teach.note: Draw a four-stage sequence on the board or show a labelled sequence. Examples in Dorset: Durdle Door (arch), Old Harry Rocks (stacks). The Jurassic Coast was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. Ask pupils to say each stage with the word 'then'.

teach.heading: Sequence in action
bullets: Crack, cave, arch, stack, stump.
The process takes hundreds to thousands of years.
New caves can start on the new headland.
teach.note: Ask pupils to order scrambled pictures. Highlight that coasts are always changing. Link to Islamic ethos by saying that the sea is one of Allah's signs and that we study it with awe and respect for its power.

practice: Number the stages in the correct order: stump, cave, arch, crack, stack.
Label the diagram of a headland with notch, cave and arch.
independent: Draw an annotated sequence showing how a stack forms.
Describe two landforms created by wave erosion using key terms.
Stretch: explain why wave-cut platforms form only along cliffed coasts.
exit: What forms after a stack collapses?
lessons.homework: Find an image of Durdle Door or Old Harry Rocks and annotate it with the stages of formation.
lessons.send: Provide a cut-and-stick sequence. EAL: use photographs with labels. Stretch: compare formation of a bay with the formation of a cove.

lessons.title: Transport and longshore drift
objectives: Describe four ways sediment is transported
Explain how longshore drift moves material along the coast
Draw and label a longshore drift diagram

keywords.def: the movement of eroded material by waves, wind, ice or rivers
the zigzag movement of sediment along a coast
the direction from which wind most often blows
small pieces of rock, sand and silt moved by water
bouncing of small stones along the sea bed

starter: Say Bismillah. Name an erosional landform.
What forms after an arch collapses?
Which type of wave has a strong swash?

teach.heading: How waves move sediment
bullets: Traction: large boulders roll along the sea bed.
Saltation: pebbles bounce along the bed.
Suspension: fine sand and silt float in the water.
teach.note: Demonstrate with a bowl of water and different sized materials: sand, gravel, small stones. Ask which would be easiest to carry. Then add 'solution': dissolved minerals carried invisibly in the water. Pupils should be able to name four methods.

teach.heading: Longshore drift
bullets: Waves hit the beach at an angle because of the prevailing wind.
Swash carries material up the beach at that angle.
Backwash returns straight down because of gravity.
teach.note: Draw the zigzag on a board. Ask pupils to trace the path of a pebble. The UK's prevailing wind comes from the south-west, so material is often moved from west to east along the south coast. Show a time-lapse of a pebble marked with a bright colour if available.

teach.heading: Net movement along the coast
bullets: Each wave moves the pebble a short distance.
Over time, material moves along the coast.
The direction depends on the wind and coastline.
teach.note: Common misconception: pupils think the sediment moves in a straight line along the beach. Emphasise the zigzag. Link to groynes as defence: they interrupt longshore drift, which builds up the beach on one side.

teach.heading: Where does the sediment go?
bullets: Eroded cliffs supply sediment to the coast.
Rivers also deliver sediment to the sea.
Sediment is deposited where waves lose energy.
teach.note: This leads into the deposition lesson. Ask pupils where they would expect the transported material to be dropped: sheltered bays, estuaries, behind headlands. Check that pupils can say why waves lose energy there.

practice: Number the steps of longshore drift in the correct order on a diagram.
Match the four transport methods with sketches and definitions.
independent: Draw a labelled diagram of longshore drift with arrows showing swash, backwash and net movement.
Write a paragraph explaining how longshore drift moves a pebble 100 m along a beach.
Stretch: predict what would happen if a pier or harbour wall blocked longshore drift.
exit: Name two ways sediment is transported by the sea.
Why does backwash move straight down the beach?
lessons.homework: Explain longshore drift in your own words to someone at home and ask them to draw what you described.
lessons.send: Provide a diagram with the arrows partly drawn. EAL: use physical movement (zigzag) to explain longshore drift. Stretch: use a map of the south coast to predict the direction of drift.

lessons.title: Deposition landforms: beaches, spits and bars
objectives: Explain why waves deposit sediment
Describe how beaches and spits are formed
Identify depositional landforms on a map or photograph

keywords.def: when material being carried is dropped because water loses energy
an area of sand or pebbles at the edge of the sea
a long narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to land at one end
a ridge of sand or shingle across a bay
an area of mud and salt-loving plants sheltered behind a spit

starter: Say Bismillah. Draw the zigzag path of longshore drift.
What is the difference between swash and backwash?
Why do waves lose energy in a bay?

teach.heading: Why does deposition happen?
bullets: Waves drop sediment when they lose energy.
This happens in sheltered bays and shallow water.
It also happens when there is lots of material.
teach.note: Contrast with erosion to correct the school-identified misconception. Waves deposit in calm places: bays, estuaries, behind headlands. Constructive waves with weak backwash also deposit. Ask pupils to say when waves are most likely to deposit rather than erode.

teach.heading: Beaches
bullets: Beaches are deposits of sand or shingle.
Sandy beaches have gentle slopes.
Shingle beaches are steeper, with pebbles.
teach.note: Compare photos of Newquay's sandy beaches with Chesil Beach's pebbles. Ask why sand is deposited in a flat gentle beach while pebbles are heavier. Mention that beaches are natural coastal defences because they absorb wave energy.

teach.heading: Spits
bullets: A spit forms where the coastline changes direction.
Longshore drift carries sediment past the bend.
Waves curve the end into a hook.
teach.note: Draw the stages: drift along the coast, a bend or river mouth, sediment deposited in sheltered water, the ridge grows into the sea, wind change curves the end, and a salt marsh forms behind. Example: Spurn Head on the Humber estuary is about 5 km long.

teach.heading: Bars and other features
bullets: A bar forms when a spit grows across a bay.
Water trapped behind it becomes a lagoon.
Loe Bar in Cornwall trapped Loe Pool.
teach.note: Sand dunes are another depositional feature: sand blown inland and trapped by plants like marram grass. Show a photograph of dunes. Ask what could happen to dunes if too many people walk across them. This links to coastal conflicts in later lessons.

practice: Label a diagram of a spit with sediment direction, curved end and salt marsh.
Sort these as erosional or depositional: stack, spit, wave-cut platform, bar, beach.
independent: Draw and annotate a spit formation sequence in four stages.
Write a paragraph explaining the difference between erosional and depositional landforms.
Stretch: explain why spits often develop near river mouths.
lessons.homework: Find a photograph of a spit or bar and annotate it with at least five labels.
lessons.send: Provide a partially complete diagram. EAL: use labelled photographs. Stretch: investigate why Spurn Head has changed over time.

lessons.unit: Unit 5: Coasts - people and the coast
lessons.title: Your holiday in Newquay: using the coast and conflicts (4.5)
objectives: Use an OS map to describe the coast at Newquay
Explain how people use the coast and the benefits of tourism
Explain conflicts of interest and suggest a win-win solution

keywords.def: when different groups want different things from the same place
meeting present needs without damaging the future
a detailed map made by the national mapping agency
visiting a place for leisure, holidays or interest
a person or group affected by a decision

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two landforms waves create.
Is a spit created by erosion or deposition?
On a 1:25,000 map, what does 4 cm on the map represent?

teach.heading: Newquay on the map
bullets: Newquay is on the north coast of Cornwall.
About 20,000 people live there all year.
Many more visit in summer to surf and sunbathe.
teach.note: Display an OS Explorer 106 extract of Newquay if available. Practise 6-figure grid references and finding the harbour, Fistral Beach, headlands and coastal paths. Common misconception from the school plan: pupils read grid references from the wrong corner; remind them the reference names the bottom-left corner of the square. Provide support sheets with the 'along then up' reminder.

teach.heading: How is the coast used?
bullets: Surfing, boat trips, walking and sunbathing.
Hotels, cafés, shops and the aquarium.
Fishing, harbour and the local economy.
teach.note: Brainstorm activities from the school plan: walking, surfing, sunbathing, boat trips and visiting the aquarium. Discuss the social (jobs, community), economic (income, businesses) and environmental (litter, erosion of dunes, traffic) impacts. Ask which uses are in conflict.

teach.heading: Who wants what?
bullets: Retired residents want peace and quiet.
Business owners want more visitors and money.
Environmentalists want to protect wildlife and dunes.
teach.note: Create four teams: retired residents, businesspeople, environmentalists, tourists. Each team writes what they want and what worries them. Highlight that these conflicts exist on every popular coast. Ask pupils to think about different views with respect.

teach.heading: A win-win solution
bullets: Zones for noisy and quiet activities.
Park-and-ride, bins and beach cleans.
Fees and rules that protect dunes and wildlife.
teach.note: Ask: can we make everyone happy? Not always, but compromise helps. From the school plan: leaders make decisions to support everyone. Link to Islam: we are stewards of the Earth and must respect the rights of people (including neighbours). Encourage careful, fair judgement.

practice: Give the six-figure grid reference for the harbour and for Fistral Beach.
In your team, write one need and one worry for your group.
independent: Describe the impact of increased visitors on Newquay (social, economic and environmental) in three paragraphs.
Suggest a win-win plan that keeps all four groups as happy as possible, and explain who must compromise.
Stretch: evaluate who benefits most and who loses most from tourism in Newquay.
exit: Name one benefit and one problem of tourism for a coastal town.
What is a conflict of interest?
lessons.homework: Write a short diary entry from the point of view of one stakeholder in Newquay during August.
lessons.send: Provide role cards with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach tourism vocabulary using images. Stretch: use evidence from the OS map to support recommendations.

lessons.unit: Unit 5: Coasts - people and the coast
lessons.title: Protecting the coast: hard and soft engineering
objectives: Explain why coasts need protecting from erosion and flooding
Describe hard and soft engineering strategies
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of strategies using the Holderness coast

keywords.def: building artificial structures to protect the coast
working with natural processes to protect the coast
a strong concrete or stone wall at the back of a beach
a wall or fence built out into the sea to trap sediment
allowing the sea to flood or erode land in a controlled way

starter: Say Bismillah. Name a depositional landform.
What is longshore drift?
Why might a village on a soft cliff be at risk?

teach.heading: Why protect the coast?
bullets: Homes, roads and farms can be lost to erosion.
Low-lying land is at risk of flooding.
Sea levels are rising with climate change.
teach.note: Show images of houses on a cliff edge. Ask: what should people do? This leads to a debate on cost versus benefit. Remind pupils that waves and storms are powerful signs of Allah's creation and humans must manage risks wisely.

teach.heading: Hard engineering
bullets: Sea walls reflect wave energy. They are strong but costly.
Groynes trap sediment and build up beaches.
Rock armour absorbs waves and is cheaper.
teach.note: Show a labelled diagram with each structure. Evaluate: sea walls last a long time (50 to 100 years) but are expensive per metre and can look ugly; groynes may starve beaches further along the coast of sediment, causing more erosion downdrift. Ask pupils to think of one advantage and one disadvantage of each.

teach.heading: Soft engineering
bullets: Beach nourishment adds sand or shingle.
Dune regeneration plants marram grass.
Managed retreat lets the sea take low-value land.
teach.note: Soft engineering is cheaper and looks natural, but may need repeating and may not protect against big storms. Managed retreat means accepting loss of some farmland or houses and compensation. Ask: is it fair to ask some people to give up land to protect others?

teach.heading: Case study: Holderness coast
bullets: The Holderness coast in Yorkshire has soft boulder clay.
It erodes by about 2 m a year on average.
Mappleton was protected with rock groynes and rock armour.
teach.note: Holderness is one of Europe's fastest-eroding coastlines, stretching about 60 km from Flamborough Head to Spurn Head. Many villages have been lost since Roman times. Protecting Mappleton (about £2 million in 1991) saved the village but increased erosion further south. Ask pupils what this shows about hard engineering.

practice: Complete a table of strategies: cost, effectiveness, effect on environment.
Sort strategies into hard and soft: sea wall, beach nourishment, rock armour, dune planting.
independent: Write a paragraph evaluating two coastal defences with advantages and disadvantages.
Explain why Mappleton's defences caused problems elsewhere.
Stretch: argue whether the money spent defending one village is justified.
exit: Name one hard and one soft engineering strategy.
lessons.homework: Research one UK coastal defence scheme and bring two facts to the next lesson.
lessons.send: Provide a comparison table with sentence starters. EAL: use pictures to match each strategy. Stretch: use cost-benefit reasoning to rank strategies for a named coastal town.

lessons.unit: Unit 5: Coasts - people and the coast
lessons.title: Decision making: how should we protect Seabourne? Unit review
objectives: Use evidence to recommend a coastal management plan
Justify a decision by weighing costs and benefits
Review learning from the whole coasts unit

keywords.def: weighing the costs of a plan against its benefits
make a judgement using evidence for and against
advice about what should be done
protecting the coast in a way that lasts and respects people and nature

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two hard engineering strategies.
What is the main disadvantage of groynes?
Explain one way waves can build a beach.

teach.heading: The Seabourne problem
bullets: Seabourne is a fictional coastal village.
It has 120 homes, a caravan park and farmland.
Its soft cliff erodes about 1.5 m each year.
teach.note: Explain that Seabourne is a made-up village used for practice. Show a sketch map with the cliff edge, homes, caravan park, farmland and a small beach. Ask: which part of the village is at greatest risk in the next 20 years?

teach.heading: Options and costs
bullets: Option A: sea wall, £6 million.
Option B: rock armour, £2 million.
Option C: beach nourishment, £0.5 million every 5 years.
teach.note: These costs are fictional and only for the exercise. Add Option D: do nothing and move the caravan park inland. Give each option pros and cons cards. Ask groups to rate each option from 1 to 5 on cost, protection, appearance and effect on neighbouring coasts.

teach.heading: Making a justified decision
bullets: Use evidence: costs, risk and who is affected.
Consider both people and the environment.
Give a reason and an alternative view.
teach.note: Model a sentence frame: 'I recommend Option B because it protects the homes at a lower cost. However, it may not look natural.' Encourage pupils to use 'however' and 'on the other hand'. Emphasise fairness: how will the decision affect the elderly, farmers and tourists?

teach.heading: Reviewing the unit
bullets: Waves and tides create erosion and deposition.
Landforms change over time.
People protect, use and enjoy the coast.
teach.note: Run a quick-fire recap with a mini-whiteboard quiz: constructive versus destructive, name the four erosion processes, order the arch sequence, define longshore drift. Highlight areas that need revision for the end-of-unit assessment.

practice: In groups, score each option for Seabourne and justify your top choice.
Quick-fire quiz: 10 questions on the unit.
independent: Write a recommendation to the Seabourne council: choose one option and justify it in a paragraph.
Complete the end-of-unit review sheet: key terms, diagrams and a six-mark question.
Stretch: write a response to someone who disagrees with your plan.
exit: State your recommendation for Seabourne and one reason.
What is one way waves create landforms?
lessons.homework: Complete the unit review sheet and list the three key terms you find most difficult.
lessons.send: Provide a scaffolded decision matrix and sentence starters. EAL: allow oral explanation before writing. Stretch: consider long-term sea level rise in the recommendation.
